problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{9}{x+2y-z}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1).$
worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b,c)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y,z)≈f(a,b,c)+∇f(a,b,c)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b,z-c⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(2,1,1)=3.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =-\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{x}(2,1,1)=-\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =-\frac{18}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{y}(2,1,1)=-\frac{18}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=-2, \\ {f}_{z} & =\frac{9}{(x+2y-z)^{2}}\,⇒\,{f}_{z}(2,1,1)=\frac{9}{(2+2(1)-1)^{2}}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(2,1,1)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(2,1,1) & =⟨{f}_{x}(2,1,1),{f}_{y}(2,1,1),{f}_{z}(2,1,1)⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,-2,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & ≈f(2,1,1)+∇f(2,1,1)\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3+⟨-1,-2,1⟩\cdot ⟨x-2,y-1,z-1⟩ \\  & =3-1(x-2)-2(y-1)+1(z-1) \\  & =6-x-2y+z.\end{aligned}
$$
